QUESTION: So it seems as though Christian attorneys are consistently told that they have to leave their faith at the door whenever they’re practicing law. As a believer and an attorney, how do you believe we’re supposed to respond to this pressure?
SECRETARY RUBIO: Remember, I did land use and zoning, okay? So – (laughter) – so no, the hardest thing to zone in the world is a church and a funeral home, as you know. So I’m telling you, nobody wants either one next to them because of the parking. But anyway. (Laughter.) No, that’s an important question. Look, I don’t – so I think your faith – attorney is what you do. Your faith is who you are. And so I think that – (applause) – and if you speak specifically about Christianity as your faith, then I would say this is a faith that teaches that your job is to care for the less fortunate, to feed the hungry, and clothe the naked, and visit the prisoner, which you’ll do often if you’re a defense attorney. (Laughter.)
And – but I – and I also think embedded in our system of government and in our system of laws is very powerful Judeo-Christian principles about the dignity of the human being and of the individual, which our legal system ultimately recognizes. If you think about our criminal justice system for a moment, it’s built on the notion that no matter how guilty someone may be, they are entitled to the most vigorous defense, and that it is the state’s job to prove the case against this person because a human life and human freedom is so valuable that you must overcome extraordinary obstacles in order to ensure that if you’re going to put someone in jail, the evidence and the burden is on your side to prove it, in essence, not the other way around.
We take that for granted, but in many parts of the world you’re presumed guilty and your job is to go in there and convince them that you’re not guilty. In our country and our system of law, you’re presumed innocent even though everybody knows you did it. (Laughter.) Right? But that isn’t because we’re nice people. It’s because embedded in our Judeo-Christian values is the belief that the individual and the freedom of that individual is something that’s sacred because it’s given to us by our creator. Our very founding documents speak to the fact that our rights don’t come from government. Our rights don’t come from the law. Our rights are not determined by whoever happens to be leading us every two, four, or six years. Our law – our rights come from our creator; they are inherent in us as a person.
So I think you bring that into the legal profession. Now, I don’t know how it applies to a real estate contract, but I can tell you how it applies to a criminal justice system and to our broader system. So I would just say that your faith should inform you in what you do. And I think ultimately it’s a faith – you spoke again that you’re a Christian. Christianity teaches us, as you – not just to care for the less fortunate but also to value human dignity and the dignity of all people, irrespective of the circumstances they come from. And I think these are things we want to encourage in the legal profession, not discourage. (Applause.)

QUESTION: So, many young Americans seem to have an anxiety about the future and are drawn to extremes, whether that be antisemitism, communism, socialism. As the son of Cuban immigrants, how do we instill the values in the next generation of love for our freedom, love for the values of our country, as you clearly have so successfully done with your own daughter?
SECRETARY RUBIO: Wow. Well, my home is not a democracy, so it begins with – (laughter) – and by the way, I was not the dictator, either. (Laughter.) I was the minister of defense. (Laughter.)
But all kidding aside, kind of – (laughter) – the – no, all joking aside, no, look, I think – look, I have no problem with people, like, going through the phases of life where they explore different thinking and so forth and so on. But I do think there are a couple things that are important that I think should be at the foundation of everything.
The first is I – and I just believe this because I think history backs it – the American story is exceptional. It’s extraordinary. It has no precedent in the history of the world anywhere. (Applause.) And I think that – I think we’ve neglected to say that. I think we spent 20 or 30 years – for combination of reasons in our education system sort of infusing in people all the terrible things that are – that have happened in the history of our country, to which I say I never said our history is perfect. I have only said our history is better than anybody else’s.
And I truly mean that. If you think about all – for example, what is a proper teaching of our history in some of its worst moments? You think about all the great justice movements in our history: the end of slavery, the end of segregation, women’s right to vote. All of these advances – every single one of them, okay – was not a rejection of our founding principles. You know what each one of them was? It was a demand that we live up to our founding principle, every single one of them. (Applause.) In fact, one of the best lines in Dr. King’s I Have a Dream speech is a demand that we live up to the ancient words of our founding. He didn’t say overthrow the government. He didn’t say reject the Constitution, walk away from the principles of the Declaration of Independence. What he was accusing us of is that we were not living up to the principles of who we were.
The second, on the point of economics – and this is just my personal point of view – look, I believe in the free market, but I don’t worship the free market. I think the market exists to serve people, not people to serve the market. The market is a tool to achieve – to provide for human achievement and prosperity. But there’s also a national interest that has to be balanced. I think the market works when it does two things: it provides wealth and prosperity, but it also provides opportunity for people to find dignified work. So we have to do a better job of understanding that there’s no absolutes here, and ultimately the market, as an example, is a tool.
I think we have to recognize that people are struggling. There’s no doubt about it. There’s no doubt, and I think the numbers are clear, that younger people today are further behind than their peers were 20, 30, 40 years ago, and to ignore that would be to close our eyes. I think we sometimes forget that yes, I’m not saying the stock market is irrelevant and unimportant, but for most people, the health of our economy has nothing to do with the stock market. The health of their economy is whether they have enough money to be able to afford the things they need and want. That’s how they judge the health of our economy.
So we do have a lot of work to make these arguments. People call it populism. I just call it common sense. I think it’s important, though, that it all starts with a founding belief – or the foundation of making these arguments is expressing to people the extraordinary story of America, and one of the things that’s most extraordinary about our history is this unbroken chain of each generation leaving the next better off, with a safer, better, more prosperous country.
And that’s the challenge before us now, because I do think there’s a legitimate fear that we will be the first generation to leave the next worse off. And that can’t happen. That’s un-American. It runs against our story. It’d run against our history. And I think the foundation for all of it is explained to people that America is exceptional but it’s not self-perpetuating. It has always required those in charge to do what it takes to keep it moving forward and that that’s what we’re called to do, and then have confidence that we can do it. It’s an enormous undertaking, and it’s – like I said in my speech, it’s something that happens over years and decades, not election cycle to election cycle. (Applause.)

QUESTION: Recently in Greece you spoke on the balance between our nation’s domestic sovereignty and our international security demands as a leader of the Western world. How can the administration adequately address both of these needs without forfeiting the support of the American electorate, which has clearly expressed a focus on domestic concerns?
SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, they’re interrelated, but they’re always going to be – look, let me start with this: I think the job of America’s government and its leaders is to work for Americans. I mean, that sounds kind of strange, but in the realm of foreign policy, we’ve almost lost it. But we’ve also lost it in the realm of economics. These are my personal views, but I’ve argued them in writing, I’ve argued them in speeches. I think there came a point at which we forgot – like, the end of the Cold War, everybody thought, okay, the whole world is now going to become free enterprise democracies, and it just didn’t work out that way. It was never going to work out that way.
The second is we placed this confidence in the markets, in global markets, and basically saying it’s okay if a bunch of jobs leave our country and relocate somewhere else. They’ll make it cheaper over there, which means prices will be cheaper over here, which is true that prices will be cheaper over here, but you just wiped out a bunch of jobs, gutted a bunch of communities, and now you have a bunch of people that don’t feel like they can move forward.
All of this happened because we lost our focus. We forgot that our job is – we’re not against the world. We’re not – our job is not to harm the world. But our number one objective must always be what’s in the national interest of the United States, and we shouldn’t feel guilty about it, okay? Next week I will get on an airplane with the President and we will fly, for example, to the Philippines for the ASEAN conference, and then we will fly to China for the APEC conference. And I was asked by a reporter the other day, well – something about a disagreement we have with China. And I said, look, the Chinese Government is in favor of what’s good for China and they don’t apologize for it.
We are the only country in the world that seems to have forgotten that. I’m on the American side of every issue. (Applause.) And – and that I even have to say that is stunning. Think about it: The fact that I even have to say that is stunning. I always remind people, I am the Secretary of State of the United States – (laughter) – not the – there was a huge outrage. We did a – we have these flags at the State Department when you walk in, and we had all these flags of all these different countries. And I – look, I didn’t go in with, like, a crusade to remove the flags. We left it there for a year and a half. But then for America 250, we made them all American flags, okay? And then we left them there after 250, and people are going crazy: Oh my God, they’re abandoning the world. I said, no, we’re not the United Nations. Take the flag; the United Nations can have all those flags. (Laughter.) It’s the State Department of the United States. (Applause.)
And so – so the way I view it is that what we need to do – I think your question was probably geared towards more why is the United States involved in things around the world. Well, we have to be involved in things around the world because whether we’re involved in the world or not, the world will be involved with us. There are things happening in other countries and in other places that do have an impact on the national security of the United States, and our economic interests as well. We can make the greatest products in the world, but if we don’t have markets that are open to us, as an example, that’s going to be a problem.
We can – if there’s instability and insecurity in our hemisphere, we will eventually have migratory pressures because this administration has made the decision that it’s going to protect our borders. But the next administration may not. (Applause.) And so I would argue that America is safer and better off if we are surrounded by countries that are stable, safe, and prosperous. But ultimately – (applause) – and we should do things in our policy because it’s in our national interest. But in the end, on any topic, the number one question we have to always ask ourselves is what is in the best interests of the United States. And we – not only have we forgotten it, we’ve actually abandoned it for far too long. And I think this administration is returning to that idea, and that’s how we try to pursue it.
Again, that doesn’t mean we don’t meet with other countries, and it doesn’t mean we don’t work with other countries, because oftentimes when our national interests align with the interest of another country, that’s where you build alliances. When your national interests are in conflict with other countries, that’s where the work of diplomacy happens, to see how you can balance the two. But in the end, if we can’t balance it, I know whose side we need to be on, and that is on the side of our people, our country, our economy, and our security. And I think that every nation governs itself that way. We forgot it, and we’re restoring it. (Applause.)
QUESTION: Thank you so much for being here. My name is Tasha Dambacher. I’m a 2L at Harvard Law School.
SECRETARY RUBIO: 2L? The rest are 3Ls. 2L, excellent. (Laughter.)
QUESTION: One of the remarkable things about the United States is that people from every corner of the world have come here, and they’ve come here not just to become residents but to become patriotic Americans. That is dependent on a shared national identity, a common civic culture, and an expectation that newcomers will embrace American values rather than simply bring the divisions of the old world with them. Today we’re increasingly reluctant to insist that assimilation is a good thing. Have we lost confidence in the idea that there is a distinct American identity that is worth preserving? And how do we restore a culture of patriotic citizenship that fosters assimilation without losing what has historically made America exceptional?
SECRETARY RUBIO: That’s a great question. That’s a fantastic question. And it’s at the heart of everything I just – (applause) – well, the first is that you’re right. I mean, and there were practical reasons why, first of all. I don’t want to, like, go into all great details, but if you came here a hundred years ago, you probably were never going back to where you came from. Just – you’re not going to get there because you’re not getting back on that ship and sailing 180 days the other way. It didn’t happen. Now you’re just a flight away, so that’s the reality; the world is more connected in that regard.
I think the other thing – some of the things that have changed about immigration – and look, I – let me start – let me preface it by saying this. It’s not that I don’t understand. If you live in a place that’s dangerous, if you live in a place that’s poor, and, like, the freest, most wealthy economy in the history of the world is nearby, I understand that allure. I get it, I really do, and I understand the human behavior. Again, I go back to our national interest. We still can’t just be a place that says you can come here from anywhere in the world that you want and you don’t have to follow any rules.
But on the point of assimilation, I think there’s a difference between coming to live and work in America and coming to be an American. They’re not always the same thing. And I think that’s incredibly important for us to remember because we do have a distinctive national character. And people ask me, though, what – we’re not – the United States, we’re not a common ethnicity. We’re not a common race. We’re not a – we’re not bound – but you know what binds us is that we’re all – I truly believe this – America as a nation – we are all the descendants of go-getters. (Applause.) If you think about whether you came here on a ship that sailed across the Atlantic, whether you came here because you refused to accept the restrictions of their nation of birth, whether your ancestors overcame the horrors of slavery and after that of segregation, we are the descendants of people that refused the limits and said we’re going to continue to strive and build for ourselves a better life. That blood literally runs through our veins. That’s who we are as a people and as a nation. And I think America will always be a nation that welcomes people from other places so long as we have certain rules and controls and restrictions in place that determines how many people can come, when they can come, who can come. Those – every sovereign nation makes that.
But to go back to your central question about assimilation and the national character, that’s absolutely essential. And look, I think it happens more often than – I think we’ve lost it in some places. I think in others it’s still very well alive. Some of the most patriotic people in this country – and this is not a criticism of anybody – but some of the most patriotic people you’ll ever meet are people that are Americans by choice, not people that are Americans – (applause) – and I’ll tell you why.
And I’ll tell you why: because of – I’ve lived in America my entire life. I was born in the United States. I’ve grown up here. I don’t know what life is like. But when you meet someone who knows what life is like somewhere else, when you meet someone that knows what it’s like to live in a society where you don’t have – not just political freedoms, but where your very future is determined on the day you are born by what your parents did and whether they were connected or not – when you meet people like that, they know that life in this country is special. They know that life in this country is different. And they have a lot to contribute.
So Americans by choice – people that did it the right way and chose to be Americans – oftentimes, I think, understand how special this country is more than someone like me, even, who was born here and lived their entire life and have never had to live under a different system or a – and I think we need to hear more from those voices as well. I think they’re very powerful in that regard. (Applause.)
QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, thank you so much for being here. We’re really grateful that you’re here. I’m Lucy Griffin. I’m a 2L. I’m the president of the Federalist Society at William & Mary. We don’t play you in sports.
SECRETARY RUBIO: No, but they have a team. (Laughter.) No, no, but they have a team. I know all about it. Go ahead. I’m like a sicko on football and college football, so I know everybody that has a team. In fact, I judge schools by their team. (Laughter.)
QUESTION: Well, we’re D2. Don’t hold it against us.
SECRETARY RUBIO: I don’t care about U.S. News & World Report rankings. Go ahead. I’m sorry. (Laughter.)
QUESTION: You’ve described – you’ve demonstrated a victorious American mentality. So at this point in the conflict in Iran, what would you consider an American victory?
SECRETARY RUBIO: That’s a great question. I think – two things that are important to understand why we’re in it in the first place. Iran has been waging – whether we want to believe it or not, they’ve been waging war on the United States since 1979. And the problem with this – (applause) – and the problem with this regime is its revolutionary nature. One thing is to be a country, because you can have disagreements with countries. The problem is the country of Iran is governed by an elected class of people who we don’t agree with, and I’m not arguing they’re moderates or people we can agree with. That’s – the government runs the country. But the country is led by a religious Shia clerical class – and not just Shia clerics but radical Shia clerics – who are motivated in their decision-making by theology.
Now, this sounds very strange, because people – that’s – you don’t often hear this conversation when it comes to geopolitics. But if you don’t understand this, you don’t understand Iran. And these people are not governors of Iran. They could care less what Iran’s economy looks like. These people are revolutionaries. If you look at the founding documents of this Islamic republic, it says that the supreme leader is not the leader of Iran. It says the supreme leader is the leader of all Muslims, including Sunni – who, by the way, don’t agree – (laughter) – and that their job is to export the revolution.
And what does “export the revolution” look like? Well, it looks like Hizballah, who they have created and funded and they helped to grow to have capabilities that rival the nation-state, and in many cases is more powerful than even the Lebanese state – the same Hizballah that blew up a bunker – a barracks that killed over 280 American Marines in 1982, ’83 and have conducted acts of terrorism to the very present day. It looks like the militias in Iraq, who as I speak to you now are plotting and have plotted for years not just to attack America but to attack regional neighbors with very sophisticated weaponry.
It looks like they’re constant sponsor – it looks like the Syrian civil war, which they were clearly behind the destruction of that country that at one time was a place that had all these different elements of society, that had Sunni and Shia and Christian and Druze and Bedouin all living along – and Alawis – all living along each other. Then it became a dictatorship supported by Iran and ultimately – and that’s the fundamental problem with them.
The second is they’re the world’s leading sponsor of terrorism. No nation-state in the history of humanity has spent more time or money sponsoring acts of terrorism around this planet than the Iranian regime, because through their proxies in Hizballah, as just an example, in our own hemisphere in the early 1990s they blew up a Jewish center in Buenos Aires, Argentina. In our own hemisphere. This is who we’re dealing with.
And these people want a nuclear weapon. And they want a nuclear weapon, and they’ll always say, oh, we’re not interested in a nuclear weapon. No, they’re just interested in all the things you need for a nuclear weapon. (Laughter.) Okay, they have built missiles for nuclear weapons. They enrich uranium well beyond the need. If what they wanted was nuclear energy, they could have had it, like South Korea has it, like Japan, like other countries do.
They argue, it’s like saying, oh, I’m not interested in committing an act of violence. I just want to buy ammunition and I want to buy a gun. But the ammunition’s not in the gun, but it would take a second to put the ammunition in the gun and become a weapon that can kill people, and that’s what they’ve done. And they have built themselves to a point where they have – over the years of neglect on this topic, we have allowed them to build up so many missiles and so many drones and so many – that they were going to hide behind that conventional shield to do whatever they wanted with their nuclear capability.
And it had to be addressed, and I know it’s unpopular. Believe me, no war is popular. No conflict, military conflict, is popular. And right now, frankly, the economic pain that we are inflicting on that regime is so great that there’s no need for military action because we’ve weakened them so much. But I think victory is ensuring that they never have a nuclear weapon. As simplistic as that may sound, I assure you that as bad as things may appear today, you think that them shooting at ships in the Straits of Hormuz is bad right now, even though 13 to 14 million barrels are getting out every night? Imagine if they had a nuclear weapon. They would hold the entire region hostage. They would hold this nation hostage.
Imagine North Korea. But North Korea is just governed by a guy that’s a little – you know, you know. (Laughter.) And – but no, no, what I mean is he’s not interested in, like, conquering Japan, okay? He just wants to survive in his regime, and I’m not excusing the terrible things that have happened there. I’m just saying. But he’s not expansionist. He’s not looking to, like, invade Japan and invade China, whatever. He’s not. These people are expansionist. They’re revolutionaries. And armed with a nuclear weapon?
The last point I would make. Every problem in the Middle East, every major problem in the Middle East – the Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia, the Shia militias that destabilize Iraq, the fighting elements that supported Assad and the destruction of Syria, Hizballah in Lebanon – everywhere you turn, there is one common denominator: the Shia clerics of Iran and their expansionist mentality. This is an extraordinary historic danger and one that cannot be ignored, because I know we think it’s half a world away, but nothing is half a world away anymore. Nothing is. It will reach eventually and threaten our country, and it’s a threat that has to be addressed, and it’s not easy to address these things because it’s not popular to address them.
But to ignore them, which would have been the easiest thing for the President to do, frankly – four years in office, leave it for the next person to worry about. But that’s what he inherited, and he said I’m not going to leave it unaddressed. But it’s hard, it’s not easy, and it’s difficult, and oftentimes it inflicts pain, economic pain and otherwise. So we recognize that.
But victory is they can never have a nuclear weapon, one way or the other. If it means they don’t have the money for one or they don’t have the equipment for one, we can never allow ourselves to live in a world – or our children or any of you to inherit a planet – in which those people who have done these things have a nuclear weapon. They have killed tens and tens of thousands of their own people, slaughtered them in the streets. Then when you’re injured, they go in the hospitals and they kill you in your hospital bed. And oftentimes, they will also kill the doctors and the nurses who treated you. That’s what they do to their own people. Imagine what they would do to us if they had a nuclear weapon. (Applause.)
Thank you. Thank you very much.

Yeah.

Yeah, I can’t comment on any of that. I just can’t comment because of the nature of it. And I also can’t comment on an internal corporate matter that’s going on with Nvidia I don’t know anything about that part of it so —

I’m not in a political office. As you know, I just don’t comment on domestic politics.

Sorry to be less than exciting with regard to that; it’s a new thing for me after having spent 14 years doing it. But I think this role is best done for the most part when you don’t engage yourself in domestic politics. I think it’s been a longstanding tradition. So —

Well, I’m not going to comment on the war – or, I’m sorry, on the elections, which is what you’re asking me about. All I can tell you is that the President of the United States identified a very real threat to this country that’s existed for a very long period of time, and he addressed it. And he addressed it even though, oftentimes, the right thing to do for the country – confronting difficult challenges for the security of our country – doing it isn’t necessarily popular but necessary. At the end of the day I think we all can all agree, I think there’s bipartisan – I would hope there’s bipartisan – maybe not anymore – but there used to be bipartisan acknowledgment that a nuclear Iran would be completely unacceptable and dangerous for the United States – not just Israel, not just the Middle East – the whole world and the United States. So I think the President took on something that other presidents have failed to do. And sometimes when you do the right thing – I don’t know if it’s popular or not, but it’s the right thing to do. And presidents are elected to do the hard things – sometimes difficult things, but necessary things.

I told you I’m not going to comment on electoral – I just don’t have any opinion on what happened in the election.

Well, the U.S. acts defensively. If there’s a threat to our forces in the region, we will act against those. If there’s a threat to shipping, we’ve been defending shipping for a while. So if there’s a clear and present threat to shipping or to our forces in the region, we have a right to defend ourselves. So all of that is determined by the threat level and whether they’re coming after us or potentially coming after us. But I mean, that’s just normal —

Well, if you remember —

Well, there’ll be talks tomorrow, starting tomorrow, in Abu Dhabi.

Oh, I’m sure. What – because here’s why. The entirety of the time we’ve been talking about Russia-Ukraine, the one thing that’s repeatedly come up is the need for security guarantees – what is the post-war security infrastructure of Ukraine and, more broadly, of the European continent going to look like? And it’s one of the key topics that’s been raised repeatedly in every conversation any time negotiations have been discussed. So I think that’s what the President is alluding to, that there’s been some advances made in what that architecture should look like post-conflict. We obviously have to get past the conflict to get to that point. So look, there’s been talks about that. I think the President was briefed on that on Thursday or Friday of last week, some of the initial thoughts that are out there. Nothing’s been finalized yet. And maybe some progress can be made in Abu Dhabi tomorrow when Jared and Steve will be there. I think they’re on the way there right now.

But you’re going to ask me anyway.

We have – we have national elections in our country every two years. I have been now involved, I guess going since 2011 when I was sworn in as a senator, so I’ve watched these things – and even my time in the legislature. It is not uncommon to have a division of power in this country. We’ve seen it before. We’ve seen elections going one direction and, a couple years later, go another. It’s just a feature of our system. So I’ve been in the minority, I’ve been in the majority, with regards to being in the Senate. I’ve been in the majority with a Republican president. I’ve been in the minority with a Democrat president. I think I’ve had every iteration of it. And the Republican continues. So we’ll do our work; we’ll continue to do our work. Congress will do theirs. I hope they do it in a way that’s responsible and focused on the issues that are important to our country and our people. But that’s our system of government. Many of our allies will be aware but they too have experienced divisions in government and divisions in their own system. So we’ll have elections again in two more years. And they could look very different; they could look the same. I don’t know. But this is the way our system works.

On – with regards to this trip? Well, they have an agenda the French have set. Obviously, we’ll be talking about super intelligence. We’ll be talking about some of the global conflicts. I’m sure they’ll have a lot of questions about the status of affairs in the Middle East with regards to Iran. I think there’ll be, obviously, a conversation. The Ukrainians are joining us; Sybiha will be there. So I’m sure that topic will come up. I know – I think they’ll be curious to know of any progress that’s being made in the technical talks that are ongoing in Abu Dhabi. And then I imagine there’s a host of other issues they’ll want to discuss. But the agenda, you’ll see it. I mean, it’s been pretty – it’s been laid out, some of the topics they want to raise and talk about. So —

No. I mean, I trust our people. I mean, we asked our people, obviously. If there was a problem, I think they would tell us. So we got to – the work must continue, right. I mean, France has the presidency. I think this is probably the last meeting in the G7 under their presidency in terms of foreign ministers. And I think we’ll host it next year. So yeah, I – if our people say it’s fine, I believe them. So —

I don’t have any progress to report to you. I think you see some of these things that are out there; you have a number of countries that continue to engage them with different ideas. But I wouldn’t say we’re in – on the verge of a breakthrough. The President would always prefer to solve this and every problem diplomatically. Sometimes that’s not possible, unfortunately. But if there’s a chance to do it, we’ll explore it. Right now it hasn’t been very productive, because the Iranian demands are simply not just unacceptable but, in some cases, outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic. All right? Let me go do my call —

Haiti?

No, I mean, the – I think – no, I mean, the Salvadorians are providing their own airlift. So there’s two things going on in Haiti. We have the gang suppression force, which is the UN mission, and they have forces – I think about a hundred soldiers that are a part of that. And that’s what we’ve been engaged in and supporting. We don’t have troops there, but we’ve been engaged. And then there’s a separate mission, which they’ve taken on bilaterally in agreement with the Haitian officials, to go after the gangs that kidnapped their forces that were there, their soldiers that were there. So that’s a separate mission. He called the President and made them aware of what he was doing, and the President understood why he was doing it. But we’re not necessarily – we’re not actively involved in that effort.

No, as long —

Yeah.

Yeah. No, as long as the chain of command is well established, who’s working for who. And I think they’ll have to – and we’ve raised this point, not because it’s a criticism, just as an observation. We have to make – we have to make sure that there’s de-confliction going on. What you can’t have is gang suppression force running into Salvadorian soldiers and shooting at each other because they think the other side are gang members. So that’s why you’ll need a de-confliction mechanism. You’ll need a lot of strong coordination because they’re operating alongside one another. So we pointed that out, and – but I don’t think it necessarily has to be a conflict. Okay?

Yeah.

Period – right.

Or – unless they can get them to change their mind and agree to reform, as they should.

They should make very clear that they do not – you still have elements of the ICC who claim that they have jurisdiction over citizens that are not – of non-member-states. And we’re never going to accept that when it comes to Americans. It’s as simple as that. We’ve been clear on that. For a year and a half, we’ve made no progress trying to get them to make that clear in their reforms. They refuse to do so, so we’re taking action. And that’s it.

Yeah, I mean, at this point, we’ve made clear to them where we stand on it and how we feel about it. And we’ve asked them, if they don’t want us to take these actions against the ICC, then they should convince the ICC to wake up and realize that they do not have jurisdiction over citizens of countries that are not members, especially leaders or a servicemember of countries that are not members of the treaty. What’s the point of the treaty? If they claim universal jurisdiction without limitation and outside the treaty, then they’re way outside the bounds of their – of the mandate that they may have from these other countries that are members of it. So it’s very simple. If they want to avoid the actions we are going to take against the ICC, they should convince the ICC once and for all to do the things that are necessary to ensure that no American servicemember or leader ever has jurisdiction from the ICC placed on them because that’s illegitimate. It’s an illegitimate action. And they refuse to acknowledge that. So we’ll do what we need to do if they don’t do it. All right.

I’m not concerned. We won’t have – we have our ways; we’ll get to it. The ICC will not be in good shape if we have to get there. And we will if we have to. But look, they still have a chance. Maybe they’ll wake up and realize that their dreams of being some universal court of jurisdiction over everyone, including countries that didn’t sign up, maybe they’ll abandon those ridiculous dreams. We’ll see. We’re on it. Okay, thanks, guys.

Homestead Air Reserve Base
Homestead, Florida
November 8, 2026
QUESTION:
Mr. Secretary —

Yeah.
QUESTION:

New York
Times
reported that you had concerns about his relationship with the Chinese spy.  Can you bring us up to date as to if Jensen Huang was cut out of any U.S. Government meetings or any briefings as a result —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Yeah, I can’t comment on any of that.  I just can’t comment because of the nature of it.  And I also can’t comment on an internal corporate matter that’s going on with Nvidia (inaudible) I don’t know anything about that part of it so —
QUESTION:
Mr. Secretary, what lesson can you take from the midterm elections (inaudible) when it comes to your foreign policy —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
I’m not in a political office.  As you know, I just don’t comment on domestic politics.
QUESTION:
Can you say —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Sorry to be less than exciting with regard to that; it’s a new thing for me after having spent 14 years doing it.  But I think this role is best done for the most part when you don’t engage yourself in domestic politics.  I think it’s been a longstanding tradition.  So —
QUESTION:
Do you agree with the Vice President when he says (inaudible) war should end?
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Well, I’m not going to comment on the war – or, I’m sorry, on the elections, which is what you’re asking me about.  All I can tell you is that the President of the United States identified a very real threat to this country that’s existed for a very long period of time, and he addressed it.  And he addressed it even though, oftentimes, the right thing to do for the country – confronting difficult challenges for the security of our country – doing it isn’t necessarily popular but necessary.  At the end of the day I think we all can all agree, I think there’s bipartisan – I would hope there’s bipartisan – maybe not anymore – but there used to be bipartisan acknowledgment that a nuclear Iran would be completely unacceptable and dangerous for the United States – not just Israel, not just the Middle East – the whole world and the United States.
So I think the President took on something that other presidents have failed to do.  And sometimes when you do the right thing – I don’t know if it’s popular or not, but it’s the right thing to do.  And presidents are elected to do the hard things – sometimes difficult things, but necessary things.
QUESTION:
Do you believe the cost of the war was worth the electoral blowout?
SECRETARY RUBIO:
I told you I’m not going to comment on electoral – I just don’t have any opinion on what happened in the election.
QUESTION:
On the two kind of active conflicts you have now, there’s been more sort of – more strikes on Qeshm Island, the —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Well, the U.S. acts defensively.  If there’s a threat to our forces in the region, we will act against those.  If there’s a threat to shipping, we’ve been defending shipping for a while.  So if there’s a clear and present threat to shipping or to our forces in the region, we have a right to defend ourselves.  So all of that is determined by the threat level and whether they’re coming after us or potentially coming after us.  But I mean, that’s just normal —
QUESTION:
And then on Ukraine, Russia-Ukraine, the President floated this idea of some kind of European-wide security pact.
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Well, if you remember —
QUESTION:
I was just wondering if this is going to be —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Well, there’ll be talks tomorrow, starting tomorrow, in Abu Dhabi.
QUESTION:
No, I mean at the G7.
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Oh, I’m sure.  What – because here’s why.  The entirety of the time we’ve been talking about Russia-Ukraine, the one thing that’s repeatedly come up is the need for security guarantees – what is the post-war security infrastructure of Ukraine and, more broadly, of the European continent going to look like?  And it’s one of the key topics that’s been raised repeatedly in every conversation any time negotiations have been discussed.  So I think that’s what the President is alluding to, that there’s been some advances made in what that architecture should look like post-conflict.  We obviously have to get past the conflict to get to that point.

QUESTION:
Mr. Secretary, I know you don’t want to comment on the elections but —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
But you’re going to ask me anyway.

— but your allies are going to ask you about it tomorrow, because it’s your first opportunity that you all meet inside the G7 after the election.

Mr. Secretary —
QUESTION:

Okay, thanks, guys.

Thank you.

So, there’s an internal process that goes on. We evaluate – anytime that there’s any sort of danger involving facilities, we instigate – we initiate an internal process that does a security assessment of our personnel, of our ability to move them if things got bad, how many people are there, dependents and the like. And then they issue recommendations done by our security folks and people on the ground. And those recommendations come to me, and it was on the basis of that recommendation that we made the decisions that we made. And it’s not just about Iran, frankly. It’s also about what’s happening in Yemen with the Houthis.

The what?

Yeah, but he’s been replaced by the vice president, who I also know, and is – I spoke to him on the plane ride here, and I’ve known him for a while, and a lot of people thought he would be the next president anyway. So obviously we’ve had a good, constructive relationship with President Peña, but there’s an internal process going on in Paraguay that we’re not involved in and we’re not going to get involved in. Our – I represent the United States of America. What I’m interested in is our bilateral relationship and cooperation with Paraguay, and I expect that that will continue to be as strong as it’s ever been and will continue to grow the way it was growing. I don’t believe this change will in any way negatively impact our relationship. And that’s a good thing, and that’s an important thing. So —

What am I sensing about what? Cuba?

That’s not the way to read it. Here’s the problem with Cuba.

Yeah, no, I know.

Well, I wouldn’t tell you if I got a result from the CIA. I mean – no, come on. But I would – because then those people aren’t going to be doing very well. So, all I can tell you is this. Here’s the problem with Cuba. The regime there is afraid of giving their people any kind of freedom, economic or otherwise, because they like to control them. So, what the regime there is trying to do, and they’ve always done, is they want to have enough economic activities just so that they are like a third-world country, but not a fourth-world country – but they don’t want to lose control over people. They don’t mind if the people don’t have a lot; they just want to make sure that whatever the people have, they depend on them 100 percent for it. That’s always been the case. How can they grow economically without losing control over their population? That model doesn’t work. And all it’s led to is millions of people leaving the country of Cuba, including many to the United States. And that has to change, because that instability and that failed state that it’s created poses a threat to the national security and national interest of the United States. So that’s what we’re focused on, is how can we get the people of Cuba more freedom – political freedom for certain, because our embargo on Cuba is codified in statute, and it requires political freedom in order to lift it; but also economic freedom. We want the people of Cuba to have what virtually – the people of virtually every country in the Western Hemisphere has, and that is the ability to go out and make a living for themselves without depending on the government to provide it for them. Even more troubling is that despite how bad things are in Cuba, there are insiders in that regime that have millions and millions of dollars stashed away in bank accounts all over the world, and that have come to – this is well documented, the military holding company GAESA, who’s been stealing what little they have from the Cuban people. So, that also can’t continue. So ultimately, our goal is for Cuba to have a better future, and we’re going to do everything we can to help put it on that path. But in the end, it will require them to wake up and realize that there is no future on the path they’re on right now, and this is a very stubborn group of people over there, but we’ll keep working on it because it’s a priority.

All right, guys. What a marathon.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio Remarks to the Press
Remarks
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
InterContinental Paris Le Grand
Paris, France
November 9, 2026
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Let’s go.
QUESTION:
How were your talks today, Mr. Secretary?
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Which one?  We talked a lot today.  (Laughter.)
QUESTION:
No, but did you mention at all the Ukraine issue with your – the other ministers?
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Well, no, because – I mean, obviously, people bring it up when they —
QUESTION:
Yeah.
SECRETARY RUBIO:
But that’ll be on the docket tomorrow.  That’s part of the program.  So today they focused on SI, we focused on global conflicts, other than Ukraine and other than in the Middle East, and then those are going to be breakout sessions tomorrow, separate sessions tomorrow.
But obviously there’s a lot of people asking about that.  As you know, our team is – I haven’t had a chance to speak to them yet, but Jared and Steve are in Abu Dhabi today on the trilateral talks, so hopefully we’ll have a good report here soon, and be able to share that with you tomorrow.  And so, we’ll see how that goes.
QUESTION:
Mr. Kushner is in favor of – I mean, he mentioned specifically that it’d be a good idea to have direct European talks with Russia.  Is that an idea you think is good?
SECRETARY RUBIO:
We’ve never been against it.  It’s been the Russians that haven’t wanted that, right?
QUESTION:
Yeah.
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Up to this point.  But they’re there.  The national security advisors for I believe Germany, the UK, and France are in Abu Dhabi, although I don’t believe they’re at the table at this moment.  But nonetheless, they’re – they’ve been involved.  They’ve been involved in all the meetings in Shell Bay as well down in Florida, so sure.  I mean, ultimately, it would be a positive, but we’ve got a ways to go.  But, no, it’s good that they’re talking – it’s good that the trilateral talks are on again.  It’s better than not having talks.  Obviously, it has to produce something and as you know, it’s been difficult to get anything productive out of that, but we’ll keep trying.  And that’s what we’ve been trying to do the whole time is try to be creative and find ways that we can help bring that conflict and that war to an end.
QUESTION:
Secretary —
QUESTION:
Mr. Secretary, Kaja Kallas today —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Look at the blue – look at that suit, blue.  That’s Gator blue.  I like it.  Go ahead.
QUESTION:
Kaja Kallas today said she wasn’t hopeful for these Abu Dhabi talks because Russia has shown no sign that it’s willing to negotiate in good faith.  Doesn’t she have a point?  Every time that the U.S. has offered economic inducements to Russia or re-engaged, they’ve just responded with more bombing campaigns in Ukraine.
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Well, look, we’re just going to keep trying.  I mean, in terms of – I can certainly tell you that your chances of success are zero if you’re not trying, so we’re going to continue to try.  We seem to be the only country in the world and the President the only leader in the world that can get the Russians and the Ukrainians to the same table.  But we recognize it will not be easy to reach an end to this.  If it was easy, we would’ve done it a year and a half ago.  This war’s almost on its fifth – going into its sixth year in February, so we – we understand the difficulty of it, but I think the President deserves credit and his team deserves credit for the amount of time they’ve put into this despite the fact that it hasn’t proven productive to this point.
At some point, this war will end, and it will end, we all believe, through a negotiated agreement.  And so we’re going to keep trying, and that’s what – that’s what’s going on today and over the next couple days.  But yeah.  No, I mean, I think if we don’t try, the chances of it working are zero.
QUESTION:
Mr. Secretary, on Jensen Huang, the President has said today that he thinks he should stay on as the head of Nvidia.  The company says there’s an investigation.  How important is it that there’s a thorough investigation, in your view?
SECRETARY RUBIO:
I’m not going to comment on an internal corporate matter for them, so I’m just not going to comment on that topic.
QUESTION:
Well, did you –
QUESTION:
The President says, in terms of the travel to China on —
QUESTION:
But it’s not – it’s not just a corporate matter.
SECRETARY RUBIO:
I don’t – you’ll have to ask the White House.  I don’t – I’m not – I don’t handle the – that part of our operation.  But I just can’t comment.  I’m not going to comment at all on the Nvidia thing.
QUESTION:
You don’t view it as a national security concern?
SECRETARY RUBIO:
I’m just not going to comment on it.
QUESTION:
Can I ask you two – I think they’ll be really —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
And I can’t, and I’m not going to, so go ahead.
QUESTION:
Really quick questions, and I know that you’ve said over and over again that everyone —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
You say you have two very quick questions?
QUESTION:
Yeah.
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Okay.  You’re going to get, like, one very quick answer.  Go ahead.
QUESTION:
(Laughter.)  I’m sure.
SECRETARY RUBIO:
I’m kidding.  Go ahead.
QUESTION:
That other countries understand how the U.S. Government works and democracy works.  We had at least two, maybe three foreign ministers today say yeah, there are questions about whether the midterms are going to change the administration’s position or strategy on it.  I understand from some of your aides that this didn’t actually come up in conversations with you, but you are aware that there are questions about whether this is going to have a —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Yeah, but I just don’t know why that’s relevant.  I mean, foreign policy will be what it is.
QUESTION:
Okay.
SECRETARY RUBIO:
And so, we – we’re not very mysterious about it.  I mean, we – I think this is a pretty forward-leaning administration.  At the – what I pointed out to you yesterday, I’ll point it out again today, and that is I’ve been involved in this for a little while now.  And while obviously Congress has a role to play in our foreign policy, the – it is the administration at the Executive Branch that leads American foreign policy and, frankly, sets it.  And when I was – when I – when we had Democratic presidents and I was in the Senate, I was reminded of that on many occasions.  We had opinions about foreign policy, we tried to influence the foreign policy, but who was – who is the president will largely – is going to determine the direction your country goes with regards to foreign policy.  And that’s the way it’s historically been in American history; that’s the way the Constitution is set up.
So again, look, Congress has a role to play in our foreign policy, particularly in what it funds and in its oversight function, but the number one factor in determining the foreign policy of the United States has always been and will remain the president of the United States.
QUESTION:
Okay.  And then secondly, just because you mentioned it in your tweet about your meeting with the French foreign ministers and a couple other foreign ministers mentioned it as well, the ICC issue.  So —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Yeah, we raise it everywhere we go, and that is the ICC is a court that continues to claim – elements of it continue to claim that they have jurisdiction over individuals and – from countries that are not members of that treaty.
QUESTION:
Right.
SECRETARY RUBIO:
And we’ve tried for a year and a half to get them to reform a nice way and they haven’t been willing to do so, so we’ll have to try a different approach.
QUESTION:
Well, what have you told the Europeans will happen or may happen if they go ahead and invoke (inaudible) the statute?
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Well, we’ve already – well, I’m not going to talk about what we might do or not do as a result of this.  Suffice it to say that we believe we can inflict tremendous damage on the ICC unless they see the error of their ways.
QUESTION:
(Inaudible.)
QUESTION:
Secretary, a member – a member of – a member of the Republican Party, Thomas Massie, minutes ago introduced a measure to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.  As the person who coordinates the interagency policy regarding U.S. national security, do you have a view regarding Secretary Hegseth’s performance as Secretary of Defense?
SECRETARY RUBIO:
I think he’s done a great job.  I mean, I’ve worked with him every single day on many of these topics.  I’ve seen the work he does and the professionalism he brings to it.  He’s very smart.  He works very hard, he puts a lot of hours into this, and on all the policy issues we’ve worked on together I think he’s done a very good job.
QUESTION:
On the topic of AI and SI —
QUESTION:
How concerning – just one question on that.  How concerning is it to you, however, that it was a Republican who introduced these articles of impeachment against —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
I think it’s unfair.  Yeah, I – look, I think it’s – I think Pete’s done a good job.  I really do.  Again, I’ve worked with him, so I see, perhaps, a side of him that the media doesn’t see, and members of Congress may not see, but I think Pete works really hard.  He’s incredibly smart.
I think he’s – not just on the issues that we’ve worked on together and the execution of them, but if you think about it, I mean, he’s carried out multiple – the Department of War and the Pentagon in particular has been responsible for many of the important things this administration’s working on, whether it’s our counter-cartel coalitions that we have going on in the Western Hemisphere – he’s done a great job with that.  I think the performance – look, the damage that was inflicted on the Iranian military structures – they have no navy, they have no air force, they’re deeply degraded from a military standpoint.  They still retain capabilities, obviously, but they are very degraded from where they were a year ago at this time.  I think the operation they conducted to capture a fugitive of American justice, Nicolás Maduro, was carried out impeccably.
So, I think from the perspective that I sit in and the seat that I am in as the National Security Advisor – and Secretary of State, for that matter – Pete has done a very good job.  He really has.  And – but obviously politics are politics and people can have different views, but I can tell you my perspective from where I sit.
QUESTION:
Can you talk about the discussions you had on AI or SI?  There’s been a big —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Well, they call it AI, we call it SI, so —
QUESTION:
Sure.
SECRETARY RUBIO:
No, look, it was – we had a conversation about it.  I think the point I made in that conversation was, on the one hand, it’s – it’s going to happen.  This – there’s no way to stop – any technological advance like SI throughout history is going to happen and it’s going to have tremendous benefits.  There are good things about it that are going to make us more productive, make individuals more productive, and improve the quality of all kinds of things.
It also has some real dangers associated with it.  We – one of the dangers people focus on is what happens if these models become independent of human control and end up taking independent actions that are harmful.  But there are other dangers to it.  The – even if it’s not a frontier model, just a good AI program that’s good enough or an SI program that’s good enough in the hands of a malign actor can allow them to do things that in the past malign actors couldn’t do.  You worry about how it can be used to create biological or chemical weapons, how to do cyber attacks on infrastructure, and carry out acts of violence or acts of terrorism that could have a huge cost.
I think we need to speak more as well about the disruptive nature that it’s going to have on our economy.  I think there will be economic benefits to SI.  I also think it will displace potentially certain industry and workers the way automation did, the way globalization did.  We need to be prepared for that as well.
So, these are all things that we have to figure out a way to maximize the benefits of SI but also mitigate the potential dangers.  This is true of any new technology.
QUESTION:
Do you think the —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
The – well, the difference between this one and the ones in the past is this one is developing so much faster than any other technology we’ve ever seen.  I mean, literally every three or two months – what you did two months ago becomes obsolete.  The pace of it is moving so fast that it’s a tremendous challenge to try to regulate or control something that’s developing faster than your ability to keep up with it.
So, it’s a real global challenge but it’s also one that the U.S. is going through, and it’s a balance between trying to mitigate its dangers and trying not to stifle innovation and advances.  And it’s a work in progress to figure out how to handle that.
QUESTION:
But does the regulatory approach being pushed by European governments at the summit – do you think it does strike that balance, or is —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
No.I mean, we’re very concerned about these global institutions trying to regulate something that would stifle innovation.  So, we don’t think that’s the right approach from our perspective.  There was a – I wasn’t on it today because I was here, but there was a phone call that I believe heads of state were on it.  Secretary Bessent represented us on that call and he expressed the same sentiment on it.
QUESTION:
Mr. Secretary —
QUESTION:
Mr. Secretary, I was wondering if you have any information – apparently the French foreign minister – I don’t know if he told you during the meetings —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
About the refrigeration attack?
QUESTION:
Exactly.  The cyber attacks –
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Yeah, he mentioned – well, we knew they were going to announce that today.
QUESTION:
And they said that it was the Revolutionary Guard from Iran.
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Yeah.
QUESTION:
Did you have any particular —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
I mean, why is that surprising anyone?  The IRGC’s been conducting acts of terrorism —
QUESTION:
Well —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
— and sabotage around the world for a long time.  That’s like, breaking news, the IRGC’s a bad group of people.  That’s why we sanctioned them.  That’s why we consider them terrorists.
QUESTION:
But on this specific issue, did the United States share any information or did you give them any information?
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Well, I would – I can’t comment on what we shared or didn’t share.  The French are quite capable certainly as well in their own intelligence field.  But suffice it to say that they put out their – today these – I mean, what kind of sickos are these people?  They attack refrigerators.  France is not even involved in this really.  I mean, if you think about it.  I mean – yet they got attacked nonetheless because this is what you’re dealing with.  You’re dealing with a deranged group of revolutionaries.
The Iranian people are great people.  I’ve said this.  Go back to my hearing when I was being nominated Secretary of State, and I talked about how great Iran is and how great its people are – and how different the Iranian people are from the small core of violent maniacs that govern them.  It’s very sick and these people are very sick, and they’re very bad people and they do terrible things around the world.  They’ve been doing terrible things now since 1979, so it doesn’t surprise us.
And so obviously the – so the news today doesn’t surprise us.  They’ve done things like this for a very long time.
QUESTION:
Mr. Secretary, can I just follow up on the question of the ICC?  Because Kaja Kallas today said that she – they had spoken to you about their continued support for the court.  Didn’t seem to be budging on your demands.  And I’m just trying to clarify, is your demand – I mean, it’s one thing saying you want a guarantee that the U.S. will not be investigated, but is the demand that nationals of any country that are not signatories to the Rome Statute not be —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Well, I care about America, okay?  Bottom line is we’re not going to have some American servicemen or American military commander standing trial at some illegitimate court that we’re not a member of.  It’s as simple as that.
QUESTION:
But I think —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
And by the way, no one raised it with me.  I don’t know if she told you – I don’t know why she would tell you that because she didn’t raise it with me and no one raised it with me, but they can if they want to and I’ll tell them exactly what I’m telling you now.  They want to join that thing, they can be a part of it.  What’s never going to happen is no American servicemember is ever going to be arrested 20 years from now because they were the fighter pilot in some operation that was conducted in a country that they claim jurisdiction over.  It’s just not – we’re not going to tolerate that.  And this is, by the way, a longstanding thing.  This is not new.  This is – there have been debates about this domestically in the United States since 2004, and it’s been going on ever since.  We’re finally going to deal with it because that court is drifting further and further into a territory that’s – into ideas that are simply not acceptable to the national interest to the United States.
So, I care – I know you’re asking about other countries.  I’m telling you I work for America, and I care about what it would mean for Americans.
QUESTION:
But if you look at someone like Duterte, who is in custody, it’s been claimed that case could —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Duterte’s not an American.  So that’s the case and they’re doing – I’m focused on the impact this could have on Americans.  I work for the United States of America.  We may agree or disagree with the way the ICC’s expressed its jurisdiction in other places.  We just view it as precedent for what they may want to do to an American in the future.  That’s what we’re focused on.
QUESTION:
Mr. Secretary —
QUESTION:
But as regards to Israel, the warrants against Netanyahu, because the President has mentioned that, obviously, but Putin —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Yeah, we think it’s an – Israel is also not an enemy, but today it’s Netanyahu, tomorrow it will be an American, so.
QUESTION:
But there’s Putin indicted as well.
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Again, it’s not about the individuals, it’s about their claim of jurisdiction over countries that are not members of the treaty.  If we wanted to be under their jurisdiction, we would have – we would have – we would have joined.  We didn’t join.  We’re not a member.
QUESTION:
There are – there are questions today about the future of the Republican party.  You have, in the past, said that if Vice President JD Vance runs —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
I’m not – I don’t know why you’re wasting your time – I’m not going to talk —
QUESTION:
— you would be the first to support his candidacy.  Does that stand today?
SECRETARY RUBIO:

QUESTION:

SECRETARY RUBIO:

QUESTION:

SECRETARY RUBIO:
In Haiti?
QUESTION:
Yes.

I can tell you that on that issue, the Canadians deserve a lot of credit.  They’ve really stepped up.  They’ve been a big catalyst in the work that’s been done.  Obviously, the United States has been very involved with them as well in this UN mission.  I think the – well, the Gang Suppression Force is starting to gain momentum.  It’s up to 2,000, with another three or four thousand that have been pledged.  So, there’s – you’re starting to see momentum in the training as well, the police force in Haiti, and improving their professionalism.
But it’s a difficult challenge.  And I would say if the Gang Suppression Force effort doesn’t work, then we’re out of ideas, so we have to make it work.  There really is no other option; there’s no plan B here anymore.  So that effort, the Kenyan-led effort, sort of just wasn’t doing enough.  This new process is what replaced it and it has to work, because if it doesn’t, I don’t know what other alternative there is at this point.  So, we’ll just continue to encourage, and we raise it at all these G7s for these countries to step up and donate money to the account necessary to make this effort successful.
QUESTION:
What’s the timeline on ramping up the number of troops deployed in the GSF?  And do you think the timeline on the elections is appropriate, just given the security situation?
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Well, look, ultimately the elections – you can’t have elections if gangs control large portions of the city, and having people say it’s not a legitimate and credible election, because if a significant percentage of the population can’t go to a voting place because it happens to be controlled by a gang, it makes it very difficult.  So, stability is important for elections to be credible.
And that’s why there are – like – and Ukraine hasn’t had an election in a long time either because they’re in the middle of a war, right?  So, our point is that we’d like to see elections in Haiti, but before you can make real progress on an election in Haiti, you’ve got to do more to push back the gangs so that people can actually go vote and not get killed or decapitated.

agrément

So, we’ll start there.  And then obviously there’s some trade issues.  I’m not our trade negotiator, but obviously our foreign policy is affected by trade, so I stay very much on top of those issues, and also have to be confronted as well.  So – but yeah, I mean, Mauro and I get along great.  I mean, we speak and we talk, but obviously there are some differences between our governments’ views on trade and some other matters that will have to be resolved.  I know Jamieson’s been working on that, and we’ll have an opportunity to interact with him.  I’ve interacted with him multiple times, many times, since I’ve been in this role.
QUESTION:
Mr. Secretary, where —
QUESTION:
Mr. Secretary, on your discussions on a democratic transition in Venezuela, do you have any sense of – at this point – of the timeline or —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
I raised it – yeah, I’ve raised it here with these groups, and we’ve encouraged more and more of these countries to be involved in that process as well.  We think they have a lot to contribute, not just to Venezuela’s recovery but the more, I think, that Venezuela is exposed to the world that doesn’t involve Russia and China and Iran, the more progress can be made there in terms of recovering, just from an economic and societal standpoint.
As far as the process is concerned with elections and the democratic transition, I believe they’re meeting again this week.  As I said, we’re on pace, if things continue on scale, to have new supreme court magistrates in place by the middle of next month, in December.  Subsequent to that, very quickly thereafter, will be the creation of the new electoral council.  These are two things that are essential.
There are three things you need for an election to work in Venezuela.  You need a new supreme court.  You need a new electoral council that’s administrative – not political – in nature, and you need a free and open press.  And I think it’s been very good that María Corina and other elements of the opposition have been in the country now for over two weeks.  No one’s been arrested.  They’re having press conferences.  They have full access to the internet.  You can’t have credible elections if the people running can’t communicate with the voters.
There’s some other things people don’t think about.  For example, there are 7 million Venezuelans living abroad.  How are they going to vote?  We need to get consulates open in the United States so that those who – that are in the U.S. are able to have a voting place they can go to.  Right now, they have no consulates open in the United States.  So, there are things like that we’ve talked about with their foreign minister – their acting foreign minister that’s in place right now.
So, I think we’re making good progress.  We just have to stay on top of it and make sure we can get these deadlines, because once you get the electoral council in place, you have these elements in place, then at that point you would hope – the expectation would be that they would declare a vacancy in the presidency, which then triggers a six-month period for an election on a date set by the legitimate electoral council that we’re hoping will be set up very soon.  So, there’s a plan.   We’re pushing forward on it.  It’s a priority for us, and I think it’ll succeed.

Do you think a democratic transition —

SECRETARY RUBIO:
Well, all of those things are – I mean, all – there’s a – I don’t think we’ve settled on a final concrete plan on what it looked like.  I think concepts have been discussed about what security guarantees could look like post-conflict.  And the reason why that topic remains in the headlines is because I think it’ll be key to ultimately being able to end the war —

QUESTION:
Mr. Secretary, was there any further discussion today on the scale of the humanitarian situation in Gaza?  There’s been very severe flooding —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Yeah, so the head of – the new head of the World Food Program, he used to work with the Department of Agriculture.  It’s now – came and gave us a brief on what needs to happen and the progress that we hope to make.  Obviously, there are agreements that were part of the ceasefire that we expect to be adhered to, and there is a growing humanitarian need that we want to address, and the World Food Program is uniquely positioned to be able to deliver that.  I think we’d like to see them continue to work out ways to work more closely with the UN program, because we think the World Food Program has the – what don’t want to see is redundancy of effort, and we don’t want to see inefficiency.
We actually think the World Food Program is able to deliver assistance in a way that perhaps the UN system on its own cannot do.  So, we’ve encouraged more coordination between the two, and that’s increasingly happening.  But – so it was raised today.
QUESTION:
On this very immediate issue, though, of getting more shelter in because there’s been terrible flooding – and I mean, five people were killed in a sandbag collapse.  You can see all the tents sort of blowing away.  I think two-thirds of the population are in tents.
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Yeah.
QUESTION:
Is there any more immediate (inaudible) —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Well, we didn’t – and I know that instance today that you’re discussing where there was some sort of a – or some sand thing that collapsed and killed somebody.  That just was in the news today; I didn’t actually see that until after our meeting.  So that specific instance wasn’t raised.
What was raised was the need for wraparound services.  In essence, food alone is not enough.  And the goal of the World Food Program, by the way, is not ultimately just to continue to feed Gaza, but to eventually have Gaza have its own ability to produce its own food, and setting up of bakeries and other things that can create food for itself so that it becomes self-sustaining.  That’s the goal we all share.  But part of that, obviously, starts with shelter and the need for heat at some point here – and obviously given the winter approaching – and all these other needs that are necessary in order to sustain life.  All of that was part of the Board of Peace program.  All of that was part of the way the ceasefire came together.  It’s in some ways fallen behind schedule for a variety of reasons, but we expect it to catch up, and a lot of good work has gone into it.  And so, we’re optimistic that we can pull that together.

We’re learning more about —

What is the future of U.S. military aid to Israel?

Well, we’re currently negotiating a memorandum of understanding.  The 10-year memorandum certainly expires.  The Israelis —

SECRETARY RUBIO:

QUESTION:
Can I ask about the UN secretary-general race?  Do you have a favorite?
SECRETARY RUBIO:
If I told you who the U.S. – if I told you who the U.S. wanted it, it would doom them to lose.
QUESTION:
That’s his next job.
SECRETARY RUBIO:
No, there’s a couple really good candidates, people that we like, two or three, and the process will work itself out.  And I think we’ve expressed our views, but that – it’s an ongoing process.  So, we don’t have, like, a candidate that’s the U.S. candidate.  We see two or three very qualified people, and we’re going to let the voting continue on that front.  And at some point the world will make a decision on who they want, and we have our opinions.  And I talked about that with President Macron just a moment ago, but I think we’re just going to keep working it the way we are right now because other countries get a vote here as well.  So, we’re watching the process closely.
In the end, what we’re interested in more than anything else is that it be someone that’s committed to UN reform.  There’s real momentum behind UN reform.  I think it’s one of the things that’s going to save the UN, is that it reforms.  If it doesn’t, it’s going to be in a lot of trouble.  And we want someone as secretary-general that’s committed, truly committed, to reform.  And that’s the standard we’re using to judge all the candidates that are out there.
QUESTION:
Are you and President Macron on board, the same views on this issue?
SECRETARY RUBIO:
I can’t represent that his views are the same as mine on – I’m just saying that we – I think – I hope France is aligned with us on the need to reform the United Nations.  And I think there’s real momentum for that.  I have not gone into a single country or spoken to a single global leader that says, oh, the UN is perfect the way it is.  I think everyone generally agrees that the UN needs – the system needs to be reformed, that there was a lot of waste, that there was a lot of bloat, and that it needed to get back to its core principles.  I think it’s troubling for a lot of people that the UN really is not at the center of any of the global crises that are going on right now.  It has not played a meaningful role in major global crises in quite a while.  So, the whole system is in need of reform.  But I think the most immediate reform that people are concentrating on is that it’s lost its core principles and sort of grown so large and bloated and gotten to areas it was never intended to tackle.
So, we’ve made real progress over the last year on reform, and I think it’s important for the next secretary-general to be someone who’s committed to continuing to make those reforms, or the UN’s going to be in a lot of trouble.  I just – I’m being honest with you.  I just think that’s the – possible if we don’t fix it.
QUESTION:
Did you discuss with Macron the future of the mission to – the UN mission to Lebanon, UNIFIL?
SECRETARY RUBIO:
We did.  No, and I think the notion is – one of the things that we’re working on from our perspective is finding the ability to monitor the implementation of the pilot zones.  It doesn’t have to be a military mission.  It could be a civilian mission.  We have some ideas.  Because it’s important – these pilot zones, the Israelis leave; the Lebanese Armed Forces are supposed to come in and take them without Hizballah retaking them and using them to launch attacks.  We need a verification system trusted by everyone and trusted by both sides that both sides are complying with their obligations under the agreements that are in place.
So, we discussed a little bit some of the ideas we have on what that could look like.  We’re not prepared to sort of discuss it yet publicly, because obviously it’s sensitive and it would require the agreement of both the Lebanese and the Israelis in order for it to work.  But we discussed that process.
QUESTION:
But that could – that can involve UNIFIL?  Because the —
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Well, UNIFIL, as you know, is expiring, so something could replace it that could – that can be in that role.  But again, the details of that are still being worked on.  And I can’t really at this moment give you – other than to say that the goal remains that we do need some credible group on the ground that can verify who is – who’s complying with what on these agreements.  And that doesn’t necessarily have to be a military mission, which is what UNIFIL was in many ways.  It was military personnel.  It could be a civilian mission, but it’s a trusted verifier is what we’re searching for.  And we have some ideas about how to achieve it, and I think France could be helpful in that regard.
QUESTION:
Secretary, have you neutralized the Iranian threat against American diplomats overseas that last month U.S. intel warned about (inaudible)?
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Have we neutralized it?
QUESTION:
Yeah, or addressed it.
SECRETARY RUBIO:
Well, look, we’re always concerned – yeah, we’ve addressed it by moving people away from the threat.  There’s a couple things that are a threat.  Obviously, we’re always worried about the safety and security of our personnel and their families overseas.  And so, when we see anything that could pose a potential threat beyond a certain threshold, we’re going to address it.  Beyond that, we’re also concerned about what’s going on with the Houthis in Saudi Arabia.  That could spiral at any moment.  In some cases, you’ve seen Saudi Arabia, for example, attack not just from Yemen, but you’ve also seen attacks come in from Iraq via the Iranian-backed militias.
So, there’s a – for us, what we always have to take into consideration is not just what’s happening now, it’s what could happen.  And if this spreads or metastasizes to other countries and airports are shut down, as an example, now we can’t get our people out and now – now they’re trapped.  So, there’s an internal process that goes on.  We evaluate – anytime that there’s any sort of danger involving facilities, we instigate – we initiate an internal process that does a security assessment of our personnel, of our ability to move them if things got bad, how many people are there, dependents and the like.  And then they issue recommendations done by our security folks and people on the ground.  And those recommendations come to me, and it was on the basis of that recommendation that we made the decisions that we made.  And it’s not just about Iran, frankly.  It’s also about what’s happening in Yemen with the Houthis.
QUESTION:
The Houthi attacks —
QUESTION:
Secretary, could I ask you about the Western Hemisphere?
SECRETARY RUBIO:
The what?
QUESTION:
Sorry.  Coming back to a question on the Western Hemisphere, Paraguay has been – under President Peña was a member of the Counter Cartels Coalition and the Shield of the Americas.  Do you have a view on the recent events and the removal of President Peña from office and the current political situation in Paraguay?
